about.title: Clearlake Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Clearlake households rely on all kinds of consumer goods, farm and outdoor equipment, and vehicle parts, and when one of those products fails, the results can be serious — a burn from a malfunctioning appliance, a fall from a collapsing ladder, or an injury from a defective tool used along Lakeshore Drive or out near Rt 53. California product liability law generally works differently than a typical negligence claim: an injured person often doesn't need to prove the manufacturer was careless, only that the product itself was defective and that the defect caused harm. That can mean a design flaw, a manufacturing error, or a missing or inadequate warning label. Multiple parties in the chain — the manufacturer, distributor, or the retailer who sold it — may share responsibility. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself; we simply connect Clearlake residents who've been hurt by a defective product with an independent attorney who can review what happened and explain the options, free of charge.

items.title: Strict Liability Can Ease the Burden
items.desc: Under California law, you generally don't have to prove the manufacturer was negligent — only that the product was defective and caused your injury. That standard can make it easier to hold a maker accountable.

items.title: Multiple Parties May Share Responsibility
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and even the retailer who sold the product can potentially be held liable. An attorney can help sort out who's responsible in your case.

items.title: Preserving the Product Matters
items.desc: Keeping the defective item, its packaging, and any related paperwork can be important to a claim. We connect you with an attorney who can advise on next steps before evidence is lost or discarded.

items.question: What counts as a defective product under California law?
items.answer: A product can be considered defective if it has a design flaw, a manufacturing error, or fails to include adequate warnings about known risks. California generally applies strict liability to these claims, meaning the injured person typically doesn't need to prove the manufacturer was careless. An attorney can review the specific product and circumstances to see which theory applies.

items.question: I still have the product that hurt me — should I keep it?
items.answer: Yes, holding onto the product, its original packaging, and any receipts or instructions can be valuable to a potential claim. Try not to alter or repair it. An independent attorney connected through LawProactive can advise on how to preserve evidence properly.
